# Introduction

Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the standard tool of population
pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and other settings where each subject
contributes a short, noisy trajectory of an underlying nonlinear
dynamical system. The challenge of estimating their parameters is
fundamentally the challenge of computing or approximating an intractable
integral: the marginal likelihood.

This vignette has three parts. The first introduces the NLME model in
the ODE modelling context that dMod2 is built for, and writes down the
marginal likelihood. The second develops the Expectation-Maximisation
(EM) algorithm rigorously, since every estimator in dMod2 is a
particular instance of it. The third covers the estimators themselves,
which differ only in how they handle the intractable E-step:

* **FOCEI** (first-order conditional estimation with interaction), in
  which the E-step is replaced by a Laplace (one-point) approximation
  at the per-subject posterior mode.
* **Adaptive sparse-grid Gauss-Hermite quadrature**, in which the
  E-step is replaced by a multi-point Smolyak rule adapted to the
  per-subject posterior, embedded in an ECM (expectation conditional
  maximisation) outer loop.
* **SAEM** (stochastic approximation EM), in which the E-step is
  replaced by an MCMC draw and the Monte-Carlo error is averaged out
  across iterations by a Robbins-Monro recursion rather than within
  them.

A further estimator integrates Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process
random effects, for deviations that are exactly zero unless the data need
them: per group, or shared by clusters of groups under the Ewens prior,
the hyperparameters estimated by marginal maximum likelihood (sections 7
and 8).

Random effects are declared on the parameter transformation as effect
formulas, `cl ~ wt + (1 + dose | p | ID)`, in the notation of lme4. A
group, a level of the grouping such as a patient or a cell line, may
own several conditions: its random effects are shared by all of them,
and its likelihood is the product over them.

The code references in this vignette point at specific entries in the
package source so that the implementation can be audited against the
math.

# The NLME model in the dMod2 / ODE context

dMod2 composes a fit problem from four named function-objects:

* `x(times, pars)` solves the ODE
  $$
  \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) \;=\; f\!\left(\mathbf{x}(t),\, \phi\right),
  \qquad \mathbf{x}(0) \;=\; \mathbf{x}_0(\phi),
  $$
  with state vector $\mathbf{x}$ and parameter-dependent right-hand
  side $f$. Code-generated and compiled to native code through
  `odemodel()`. Hereafter $f$ is reserved for this RHS.
* `g(...)` is the *observation function* mapping the ODE solution to
  observables,
  $$
  g\!\left(\mathbf{x}(t; \phi)\right) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{d_y}.
  $$
  Concentrations, transformed states, ratios, sums; whatever the
  experiment actually measures. Hereafter $g$ is reserved for this
  observation map.
* `p(...)` is the *parameter transformation* mapping outer parameters
  to inner ODE/observation parameters. For NLME this is exactly the
  place where the population structure
  $\phi_i = h(\theta, \eta_i)$ enters: after
  `insert(trafo, "x <- exp(x)", x = "cl")` the effect formula
  `cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID)` replaces `cl` in every condition of subject $i$ by
  $\theta_{cl} + \eta_{cl,i}$, so $\phi_{i,cl} = \exp(\theta_{cl} + \eta_{cl,i})$
  (`R/randomEffects.R`).
* `errfn` defines the residual variance structure, with
  $\sigma(\phi_i, t_{ij})$ optionally depending on parameters and time.

The composed prediction function $g \circ x \circ p$ produces, for
subject $i$ at time $t_{ij}$,

$$
\mu_{ij}(\psi, \eta_i) \;=\; g\!\left(\mathbf{x}\!\left(t_{ij};\, h(\theta, \eta_i)\right)\right),
$$

and the observation model is

\begin{equation}
y_{ij} \;=\; \mu_{ij}(\psi, \eta_i) \;+\; \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\, \sigma^2(\phi_i, t_{ij})\right),
\qquad \eta_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\, \Omega\right).
\label{eq:nlme}
\end{equation}

The population parameters are $\psi = (\theta, \Omega, \sigma)$. The
NLME-specific parts of \eqref{eq:nlme}, the random effects $\eta_i$
and the covariance $\Omega$, sit *outside* the ODE: $f$ does not see
$\eta_i$ at all; $\eta_i$ only enters through
$\phi_i = h(\theta, \eta_i)$, which is what `p()` evaluates. This
separation matters for two reasons:

1. Sensitivities $\partial \mu_{ij} / \partial \eta_{i,k}$ come from
   the standard dMod2 sensitivity pipeline composed via the chain rule
   $\partial \mu / \partial \eta = \partial g / \partial x \cdot \partial x / \partial \phi \cdot \partial \phi / \partial \eta$.
   No separate machinery is needed for the random effects.
2. The marginal likelihood (next section) factorises over subjects
   because each $\eta_i$ couples only to $y_i$ via the ODE and back to
   the population through the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \Omega)$.

The marginal log-likelihood is, summing over subjects,

\begin{equation}
\ell(\psi) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \log L_i(\psi),
\qquad
L_i(\psi) \;=\; \int p\!\left(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi\right) \, p\!\left(\eta_i \mid \Omega\right) \, d\eta_i.
\label{eq:marginal}
\end{equation}

For an ODE-based $\mu_{ij}$ this integral has no closed form. Every
NLME estimator is a particular strategy for approximating
\eqref{eq:marginal} cheaply enough to be evaluated thousands of times
during outer optimisation while still being faithful enough to recover
the true maximum.

Here $y_i$ is the data of all conditions of group $i$. Conditions that
belong to no group, reference conditions for example, add their data
$-2 \log$-likelihood as it is.

In code, the integrand of \eqref{eq:marginal} is the objective of the
data, `normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = err)`, which provides
$-2 \log p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)$ summed over the conditions, plus
the prior of the random effects, $\sum_i \eta_i^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_i +
N \log |\Omega|$, which `em()` builds from `randomEffects(p)`
(`R/nlmePrior.R::.normalPrior`). Their sum is the joint $-2 \log$
density $-2 \log p(y, \eta \mid \psi)$ up to a constant that every
estimator consumes. The estimation design, which conditions belong to
which group and which etas they share, is assembled once by
`R/nlmeDesign.R::.emDesign`.

# The Expectation-Maximisation algorithm

The marginal likelihood \eqref{eq:marginal} couples observed data $y$
and latent variables $\eta$. EM is the canonical algorithm for
maximising likelihoods of this form. Both FOCEI and the quadrature
method are particular approximations of it; we therefore develop EM
in full first, then specialise.

## Jensen's lower bound

Pick any reference parameter value $\psi^{(t)}$ and let
$q_i(\eta_i) \;=\; p(\eta_i \mid y_i, \psi^{(t)})$ be the posterior of
$\eta_i$ given the data under $\psi^{(t)}$. For any other $\psi$,

\begin{align*}
\log L_i(\psi)
\;&=\; \log \int q_i(\eta_i) \, \frac{p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)}{q_i(\eta_i)} \, d\eta_i \\
\;&\geq\; \int q_i(\eta_i) \, \log \frac{p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)}{q_i(\eta_i)} \, d\eta_i
&&\text{(Jensen)} \\
\;&=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_i}\!\left[\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)\right]}_{Q_i(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})}
\;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_i}\!\left[\log q_i(\eta_i)\right]}_{\text{entropy, independent of }\psi}.
\end{align*}

The inequality is *tight* when $\psi = \psi^{(t)}$, because then
$p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi) / q_i(\eta_i) = p(y_i \mid \psi^{(t)})$,
which is constant in $\eta_i$ and Jensen becomes an equality.

Summing across subjects, the population $Q$-function is

$$
Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)}) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N Q_i(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})
\;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{q_i}\!\left[\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)\right].
$$

## The EM iteration

EM alternates between

* **E-step:** at $\psi^{(t)}$, evaluate $q_i = p(\eta_i \mid y_i, \psi^{(t)})$
  and assemble $Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$ as a function of $\psi$.
* **M-step:** $\psi^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\psi Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$.

## Monotone improvement

The EM iterate never decreases the marginal log-likelihood. From the
Jensen bound,

$$
\ell(\psi^{(t+1)}) \;\geq\; Q(\psi^{(t+1)} \mid \psi^{(t)}) - \mathcal{H}(q)
\;\geq\; Q(\psi^{(t)} \mid \psi^{(t)}) - \mathcal{H}(q)
\;=\; \ell(\psi^{(t)}),
$$

where the first inequality is Jensen at $\psi^{(t+1)}$, the second
follows from the M-step (since $\psi^{(t+1)}$ maximises $Q$, and
$\mathcal{H}(q) = -\mathbb{E}_q \log q$ does not depend on $\psi$),
and the equality is tightness at $\psi = \psi^{(t)}$. Strict
improvement unless the current iterate is already a stationary point
of $\ell$.

## Expectation Conditional Maximisation (ECM)

When the M-step is itself a hard nonlinear problem, but $\psi$ splits
into blocks $\psi = (\psi_A, \psi_B)$ such that the conditional
updates $\psi_A \mid \psi_B$ and $\psi_B \mid \psi_A$ are easy,
replace the M-step with a sequence of conditional maximisations:

* **CM-1:** $\psi_A^{(t+1)} \;=\; \arg\max_{\psi_A} \; Q\!\left((\psi_A, \psi_B^{(t)}) \mid \psi^{(t)}\right)$.
* **CM-2:** $\psi_B^{(t+1)} \;=\; \arg\max_{\psi_B} \; Q\!\left((\psi_A^{(t+1)}, \psi_B) \mid \psi^{(t)}\right)$.

Each CM step still increases $Q$, hence each ECM cycle still increases
$\ell$. The blockwise structure is critical for NLME models where the
variance component $\Omega$ admits a closed-form conditional update
from sufficient statistics while the structural parameters $\theta$
do not.

## Specialising to NLME

In our setting
$\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi) = \log p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi) + \log p(\eta_i \mid \Omega)$,
both pieces depend on $\psi$, and the latent posterior is the
nonstandard

$$
q_i(\eta_i) \;\propto\; p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi^{(t)}) \, p(\eta_i \mid \Omega^{(t)}).
$$

Two things make this difficult:

1. The E-step expectation
   $\mathbb{E}_{q_i}[\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)]$ is, as a function
   of $\psi$, an integral against a posterior that itself has no closed
   form because $p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)$ runs through the nonlinear
   ODE solution.
2. The M-step still needs derivatives of $Q$ to drive a population
   solver.

Every NLME estimator is a recipe for replacing the intractable E-step
expectation with something computable. Three natural categories, each
developed in its own chapter below:

* **Deterministic, low-order:** approximate $q_i$ by a Gaussian
  centred at its mode and replace the expectation by a one-point rule
  at that mode. This is FOCEI (`method = "focei"`); the same rule
  driving a plain EM outer loop is `method = "laplaceEM"`.
* **Deterministic, high-order:** approximate the expectation by a
  multi-point quadrature rule adapted to the local Gaussian
  approximation of $q_i$. This is the sparse-grid Gauss-Hermite path
  (`method = "quadrature"`).
* **Stochastic:** replace the expectation by a Monte Carlo average
  drawn from $q_i$ via MCMC, averaged across iterations rather than
  within them. This is SAEM (`method = "saem"`).

# FOCEI

## Laplace approximation in the E-step

Fix $\psi$ and define, in dMod2's convention of $-2 \log$ densities,
the joint objective of group $i$

$$
\Phi_i(\eta) \;\equiv\; -2\log p\!\left(y_i \mid \eta, \psi\right) -2\log p\!\left(\eta \mid \Omega\right).
$$

Let $\hat\eta_i = \arg\min_\eta \Phi_i(\eta)$ and
$H_i = \nabla^2_\eta \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)$, so the posterior precision is
$P_i = H_i / 2$. Expanding $\Phi_i$ to second order around
$\hat\eta_i$ and integrating the Gaussian gives the Laplace
approximation

\begin{equation}
L_i(\psi) \;\approx\; (2\pi)^{K/2} \, |P_i|^{-1/2} \, \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)\right)
\label{eq:laplace}
\end{equation}

and the objective value of the group

$$
\mathrm{OFV}_i(\psi) \;\approx\; \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) \;+\; \log |H_i / 2| \;-\; K \log(2\pi).
$$

The prior term of $\Phi_i$ is written without its $K \log(2\pi)$, which
cancels the last term, so dMod2 minimises
$F(\psi) = \sum_i [\Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log|H_i/2|]$ plus the data of the
conditions without a group, the full $-2\log L$ with every constant of
the data.

The "I" in FOCEI is the *interaction* between the random effects and
the residual variance: $H_i$ contains the derivatives of $\sigma$ in
$\eta$, which couple structural and error-model contributions. Methods
that drop this coupling (FOCE without I) lose accuracy whenever
$\sigma$ depends on $\eta$.

## Why this is approximate EM

In the EM language of section 4, FOCEI uses a one-point rule for the
E-step expectation: $q_i$ is approximated by the local Gaussian
$\tilde q_i(\eta_i) = \mathcal{N}(\eta_i \mid \hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$ and
the expectation by a single evaluation at $\hat\eta_i$ plus the
normalising factor $\log |P_i|$. The M-step becomes a single combined
optimisation over $\psi$, since the surrogate is an analytic function.
The conditional standard errors of the random effects reported by a
fit are the square roots of the diagonal of $P_i^{-1} = 2 H_i^{-1}$.

| EM ingredient | FOCEI approximation |
|---|---|
| posterior $q_i(\eta_i) = p(\eta_i \mid y_i, \psi)$ | Gaussian centred at $\hat\eta_i$ with covariance $(H_i/2)^{-1}$ |
| E-step expectation | Laplace one-point rule at $\hat\eta_i$ with $\log |H_i/2|$ correction |
| M-step | gradient-based outer optimisation of $F(\psi)$ |

## Bilevel optimisation

FOCEI is a bilevel problem (`R/nlmeFocei.R::.fitFocei`). Per call to the
outer objective at $\psi$:

1. **Inner loop** (one trust-region solve per group) finds
   $\hat\eta_i(\psi) = \arg\min_\eta \Phi_i(\eta; \psi)$ over the rows of
   all conditions of the group, warm-started from the previous outer
   iteration and shifted to first order along the outer step. The step
   model is the Gauss-Newton Hessian plus an SR1 correction learned from
   the gradients of accepted steps, the curvature of the prediction in the
   etas that Gauss-Newton drops, wherever the sum stays positive definite;
   $H_i$ itself stays Gauss-Newton. An eigen-floor
   $$
   \lambda_k(H_i) \;\leftarrow\; \max\!\left(\lambda_k(H_i),\; \varepsilon\right),
   \qquad \varepsilon \;=\; 10^{-10} \frac{\operatorname{tr} H_i}{K},
   $$
   keeps $\log |H_i|$ defined where the local curvature is degenerate.

2. **Outer gradient** by the envelope theorem: $\hat\eta_i$ minimises
   $\Phi_i$, so its shift contributes nothing to
   $\nabla_\psi \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)$,
   $$
   \nabla_\psi F \;=\; \sum_i \nabla_\psi \Phi_i\big|_{\eta=\hat\eta_i} \;+\; \sum_i \frac{d \log |H_i|}{d \psi},
   $$
   the second term from section 5.4. The inner trust stops on the change
   of its value, so the eta gradient $g_i$ it leaves is of the order of
   the square root of its tolerance times the curvature; the first term
   takes the Newton correction to the exact mode,
   $-\Phi_i^{\psi\eta} H_i^{-1} g_i$, with which its error is of second
   order.

3. **Outer Hessian**: the exact Schur complement of the joint Hessian
   at the modes (second derivatives of the prediction),
   $$
   \nabla^2_\psi F \;\approx\; \sum_i \left[ \Phi_i^{\psi\psi} - \Phi_i^{\psi\eta} \left(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}\right)^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi} \right],
   $$
   plus the Gauss-Newton Hessian of the volume term.

4. **Outer trust region** takes the step on $F(\psi)$, the modes are
   kept as warm starts, and the loop repeats. A rejected step shrinks the
   radius to a quarter of the radius or of the step, whichever is shorter,
   in the inner and the outer trust region alike.

## The volume term

The inner Hessian is the Gauss-Newton form, over the rows $r$ of the
group with the Hessian $L_r$ of the row loss in prediction and sigma,
$$
H_i \;=\; \sum_r J_r^{\!\top} L_r J_r \;+\; 2\, \Omega^{-1},
\qquad J_r = \partial(\mu_r, \sigma_r) / \partial \eta,
$$
so the derivative of $\log |H_i|$ is not delivered by the inner solve.
`R/nlmeFocei.R::.foceiVolume` evaluates it in closed form,

$$
\frac{d \log |H_i|}{d \psi_k}
\;=\;
\operatorname{tr}\!\left(H_i^{-1}\, \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \psi_k}\bigg|_\eta\right)
\;+\;
\sum_l \operatorname{tr}\!\left(H_i^{-1}\, \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \eta_l}\right) \cdot \frac{d \hat\eta_l}{d \psi_k},
$$

with $d \hat\eta / d \psi$ from the implicit function theorem on the
exact joint Hessian. Its Hessian leaves out third-order sensitivities
and $d^2\hat\eta / d\psi^2$; in the direction of $\Omega$ that is a
large error when $\sigma$ depends on $\eta$, where the quadrature
Hessian is the better one.

### Which sensitivities are required

$\partial H_i / \partial \psi_k$ needs $\partial^2 \mu / (\partial \eta\, \partial \psi_k)$
and $\partial H_i / \partial \eta_l$ needs $\partial^2 \mu / (\partial \eta\, \partial \eta_l)$,
the same for $\sigma$: mixed *second-order* sensitivities, from the
`deriv2` pipeline (`odemodel(..., deriv2 = TRUE)`, `Y(..., deriv2 = TRUE)`,
`P(..., deriv2 = TRUE)`). Third-order sensitivities are not required,
which is what the Gauss-Newton form buys.

### Forward over reverse

Every second derivative the volume term uses is a contraction: a trace
$\operatorname{tr}(M\, \partial H_i / \partial x)$ with a fixed matrix $M$,
or the joint Hessian applied to an $\eta$ direction. With
`control = list(derivMode = "forward-reverse")`, the default, `em()` gets
them from directional sweeps instead of the full second-order
sensitivities (`R/nlmeSweeps.R`); the models are built with
`derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`.

The etas of different groups never meet in a condition, so the $k$-th
eta of every group shares one tangent $v_k$: one forward pass along
$K$ tangents for all groups. A backward sweep with the seed $w$ on the
predictions and sigmas of the rows, and $\dot w_k$ along tangent $k$,
returns $J^\top w$ and
$\sum_r w_r \nabla^2 f_r\, v_k + J^\top \dot w_k$ for every $k$.

- The **eta rows of the joint Hessian** come from one sweep with the
  loss gradient as seed and its derivative $L_r J_r v_k$ along tangent
  $k$. They give $\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}$, $\Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$ and the mode
  shift $d\hat\eta/d\psi = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$.
- The **trace gradients** are linear in $M$. Seed $j$ is
  $2 L_r J_{r,j}$, and along tangent $k$ the derivative of $L_r$
  contracted with $J_{r,j}$ and $J_{r,k}$. Its slice $k$ is $U_{jk}$, and
  $$
  \nabla \operatorname{tr}(M H_i) \;=\; \sum_{j,k} M_{jk}\, U_{jk}
  $$
  for every symmetric $M$: $K$ seeds for any number of matrices.

The eta rows and the $K$ trace seeds go back in one sweep: the trailing
axis of every cotangent holds $K + 1$ blocks, a seed and its derivatives
along the tangents each, which cppDE and the compiled observation and
parameter functions solve together.

The volume gradient takes $M = H_i^{-1}$. The derivatives of $H_i$
itself come from the unit matrices $M = E_{kl}$; they give the volume
curvature
$$
-\operatorname{tr}\!\left(H_i^{-1} D_a H_i\, H_i^{-1} D_b H_i\right)
+ \operatorname{tr}\!\left(H_i^{-1}\, \partial^2_{ab} 2\Omega^{-1}\right),
$$
which is exact for models linear in the etas. The outer trust region
takes the Gauss-Newton Schur complement, this curvature in the rows and
columns of the variance parameters and a BFGS correction from successive
exact volume gradients. Between structural parameters the term from the
curvature of the prediction is missing, so there only BFGS learns the
volume curvature. The reported Hessian is the exact forward-over-forward
one where the model also has `deriv2`. Otherwise it is the exact Schur
complement of the joint Hessian, from one sweep along the outer
parameters and the etas, with the volume curvature above.
`summary()` says which one it is.

## The C++ FOCEI kernel

The bilevel orchestration runs in C++ (`src/focei_kernel.cpp`). The
inner trust region of a group inlines the residual of each of its
condition blocks, the Gauss-Newton Hessian with the
$\partial \sigma / \partial \eta$ contribution, and the MVN $\eta$-prior,
without `normL2` per call; the trial points of all groups go out as one
batched prediction per round. Model
and error functions are still invoked via R (they wrap compiled
native code anyway), but the per-iteration glue is gone. Multi-output
models and $\eta$-dependent $\sigma$ (proportional or combined error
models) are handled in the same loop: the kernel reads
$\partial \sigma / \partial \eta$ from the error model's `deriv`
attribute and propagates it through the per-row gradient and
Hessian.

# Adaptive sparse-grid quadrature

## Why move beyond Laplace

Recall from section 4 that the E-step has to evaluate the per-subject
marginal likelihood

$$
L_i(\psi) \;=\; \int p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)\, p(\eta_i \mid \psi)\, d\eta_i
\;=\; \int e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\eta;\psi)} \, d\eta,
$$

a $K$-dimensional integral with no closed form because the inner
likelihood runs through the nonlinear ODE. The Laplace approximation
\eqref{eq:laplace} replaces this integral by a single evaluation at
$\hat\eta_i$ plus a $\log|H_i|$ curvature correction, i.e. it treats
$\Phi_i$ as locally quadratic. Its error is $O(K / n_i)$ per subject
and is dominated by the third and fourth derivatives of $\Phi_i$ at
the mode. Two practical scenarios where this matters:

* Datasets with informative-but-short trajectories (oral PK at the
  absorption limit, sparse sampling near saturation) where $\Phi_i$
  is noticeably skewed.
* Variance components $\Omega$ that are themselves the target of
  inference. Laplace systematically over-estimates the marginal
  likelihood because $|H_i|^{-1/2}$ overweights the peak relative to
  the tails, which biases $\Omega$ downward.

The fix is to replace the one-point Laplace rule with a multi-point
*cubature rule* that approximates the same integral by

$$
\int e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\eta)}\, d\eta \;\approx\; \sum_{b=1}^{B} W_b \, e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\eta_b)},
$$

evaluated at $B$ nodes $\eta_b$ with weights $W_b$. A well-designed
rule is exact whenever the integrand is a polynomial in $\eta$ times a
Gaussian of bounded degree, recovers Laplace as a single-node special
case, and converges at a rate set by the regularity of $\Phi_i$. The
remaining design question is how to pick $\{(\eta_b, W_b)\}$ so that
the node count $B$ does not blow up with the random-effect dimension
$K$. That is exactly what the Smolyak construction addresses.

## Smolyak sparse grids of nested rules

### Nested one-dimensional rules

The physicists' Gauss-Hermite rule with $m$ nodes approximates the
Gaussian-weighted 1D integral

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(z)\, e^{-z^2}\, dz \;\approx\; \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j\, g(z_j)
$$

exactly whenever $g$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2m - 1$. Its
node sets of different sizes do not contain each other. Genz and Keister
(1996) extend the three-point rule by Kronrod-Patterson steps to a
nested sequence of 1, 3, 9, 19 and 35 points, exact to degree 1, 5, 15,
29 and 51: every rule holds the nodes of the previous one, so a higher
level reuses every evaluation of the lower one. The nodes and weights
are computed once in 300-bit arithmetic.

### Why tensor products are not enough

Lifting to $K$ dimensions by *tensor product* puts a node at every
combination of the 1D nodes and multiplies the weights. The rule is
exact in *each coordinate separately* but uses $m^K$ nodes: for $K = 5$
random effects and $m = 7$ that is $16{,}807$ ODE solves per group per
outer gradient call. A polynomial of *total* degree $d$ has far fewer
monomials than the full product space, but the tensor rule pays for all
of them.

### The Smolyak combination

The sparse-grid construction is not new: Smolyak (1963) introduced the
combination rule, Heiss and Winschel (2008) developed sparse-grid
quadrature for the likelihood of random-coefficient models, and Clausen,
R{\o}nn and Skovgaard (2009) applied adaptive sparse-grid Gaussian
quadrature to nonlinear mixed-effects models. What dMod2 contributes is
its integration into a pipeline that propagates *exact* analytic
gradients and Hessians of the marginal likelihood through the ODE
sensitivity chain, so the sparse-grid E-step is differentiated rather
than finite-differenced.

With $\Delta^l = \mathcal{U}^l - \mathcal{U}^{l-1}$ the difference of the
1D rules of levels $l$ and $l - 1$, the level-$L$ sparse rule
($L \geq K$) is

$$
A(L, K) \;=\; \sum_{|\mathbf{i}| \leq L} \Delta^{i_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \Delta^{i_K},
$$

where $\mathbf{i} = (i_1, \dots, i_K)$ controls how many nodes are spent on
each coordinate (`src/quadrature.cpp::sparseGridGK`, `R/nlmeQuadrature.R::.sparseGrid`).
The level $L$ is a single accuracy knob:

* **Polynomial accuracy.** $A(L, K)$ integrates every polynomial of
  total degree $2(L - K) + 1$ exactly against the Gaussian weight.
* **Cost.** The nodes grow polynomially in $K$ at fixed $L - K$. For $K = 3$
  the levels 3 to 7 have 1, 7, 19, 45 and 117 nodes; for $K = 4$ the
  levels 6 and 7 have 29 and 89, against 49 and 201 for the
  non-nested Gauss-Hermite grid.
* **Laplace as a limit.** At $L = K$ the rule is a single node, which after
  the affine change of variable in the next subsection coincides with
  Laplace. Each level above probes more of the non-Gaussian tails.

### Why the weights are signed

The difference rules make some weights $W_b$ negative, and the proof of
polynomial exactness goes through on the signed combination. The
per-group log-likelihood

$$
\log L_i \;\approx\; \log \!\left| \sum_b W_b\, e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\eta_b)} \right|
$$

is therefore aggregated in log space *with explicit sign tracking*, the
signed log-sum-exp below.

## Adapting to the local posterior

The Smolyak rule of the previous subsection lives in a standard
reference frame: its nodes integrate against the weight
$\exp(-\mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{z})$ on $\mathbb{R}^K$. The E-step
integral we actually need is

$$
L_i(\psi) \;=\; \int e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}\Phi_i(\eta;\psi)} \, d\eta,
$$

so the rule has to be transported from $z$-space onto a subject- and
$\psi$-specific grid in $\eta$-space. The natural choice is the
local Gaussian approximation $\mathcal{N}(\hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$, $P_i = H_i/2$, that
the FOCEI machinery already computes for free: it is the best
quadratic match to $\Phi_i$ at the mode, and using it as the
$z \to \eta$ map is what makes the quadrature *adaptive*. Every outer
iteration produces fresh $(\hat\eta_i, P_i)$, the nodes follow, and
the rule remains well-centred even as $\psi$ moves through the
optimisation.

Let $L_H$ be the lower Cholesky factor of the posterior precision $P_i$. The affine change of
variable

$$
\eta \;=\; \hat\eta_i + \sqrt{2} \, L_H^{-\top} \mathbf{z}
$$

is precisely the map that sends a standard normal in $z$ onto
$\mathcal{N}(\hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$ in $\eta$ (the $\sqrt 2$ converts
between the physicists' weight $e^{-z^2}$ and the probabilist
$e^{-z^2/2}$). It folds the Jacobian $2^{K/2} / |\det L_H|$ together
with the implicit $\exp(\mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{z})$ back-correction
into augmented weights,

$$
\log |W_b| \;=\; \tfrac{K}{2} \log 2 \;-\; \log |\det L_H| \;+\; \log |w_b^{\mathrm{GH}}| \;+\; \mathbf{z}_b^\top \mathbf{z}_b,
$$

with the sign of $w_b^{\mathrm{GH}}$ tracked separately.
`R/nlmeQuadrature.R::.quadratureNodes` performs this transform. The
result is the per-subject grid that the E-step expectation is taken
against: it puts most of its mass where the posterior actually lives,
returns exact answers when $e^{-\Phi_i/2}$ is a polynomial in $\eta$
times the local Gaussian, and reduces gracefully to Laplace at the
lowest level $L = K$ (a single node at $\hat\eta_i$ with weight equal
to the Laplace normaliser).

## Signed log-sum-exp aggregation

For numerical stability the per-subject log-likelihood is built in
log space. For nodes $b = 1, \dots, B$ define

$$
\ell_b \;=\; \log |W_b| \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2} \Phi_i(\eta_b),
\qquad
s_b \;=\; \operatorname{sgn}(W_b).
$$

Then

$$
\log L_i \;=\; \log \!\left| \sum_b s_b \exp \ell_b \right|
\;=\; M_i \;+\; \log \!\left| \sum_b s_b \exp(\ell_b - M_i) \right|,
\qquad M_i \;=\; \max_b \ell_b.
$$

Downstream moments use the same softmax weights with the sign kept,

$$
w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b \;=\; s_b \exp(\ell_b - \log L_i),
\qquad
\hat m_i \;=\; \sum_b w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b \, \eta_b,
\qquad
\hat M_i \;=\; \sum_b w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b \, \eta_b \eta_b^\top.
$$

If $\sum_b s_b \exp(\ell_b - M_i)$ is non-positive or non-finite, the
grid is under-resolved: the evaluator stops and names the group, and a
higher level resolves it. The effective sample size
$1 / \sum_b (w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b)^2$ is exported in the per-subject
diagnostics so grid adequacy can be monitored per subject.

`R/nlmeQuadrature.R::.nodeSum` implements this aggregation, including the
gradient and Hessian pieces below.

## Gradient and Hessian through the integral

The marginal log-likelihood gradient is, at node level,

$$
\nabla_\psi \log L_i \;=\; \sum_b w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b \, \nabla_\psi \ell_b,
\qquad
\nabla_\psi \ell_b \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2} \nabla_\psi \Phi_i(\eta_b),
$$

a softmax-weighted average. The Hessian uses the log-sum-exp identity

$$
\nabla^2_\psi \log L_i \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_b w^{\mathrm{sm}}_b \, \nabla^2_\psi \ell_b}_{\text{average Hessian}} \;+\; \underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}_{w^{\mathrm{sm}}} (\nabla_\psi \ell_b)}_{\text{spread term}},
$$

where the covariance is taken with $w^{\mathrm{sm}}$ as a signed
probability measure,
$\operatorname{Cov}(g) = \mathbb{E}[g g^\top] - \mathbb{E}[g]\mathbb{E}[g]^\top$.
The identity is algebraically exact for signed weights (it uses only
that the weights sum to one).

Per-node $\nabla_\psi \ell_b$ and $\nabla^2_\psi \ell_b$ come from one
prediction over all groups, nodes and conditions and one call of the
normL2 kernel (`.nodeData`).
dMod2's existing analytical sensitivity chain through the ODE solver
supplies the derivatives, so the quadrature kernel itself emits pure
numbers and does not need to know anything about the model.

## Fit on frozen nodes

Optimising $\psi$ with the modes recomputed at every trial point would
relocate the grid constantly; keeping it frozen for good would optimise
the wrong objective. `R/nlmeQuadrature.R::.fitQuadrature` alternates the
two:

1. **Rebuild.** At the current $\psi$ the inner trust of the FOCEI kernel
   finds every $\hat\eta_i(\psi)$ and $H_i$, and the adapted grid of each
   group is placed. The level of a group is the lowest from its stage up
   whose next level changes its $-2\log L_i$ by at most `tol` over the
   number of groups (`control$quadrature$tol`, default 0.1); levels are
   never lowered, so the objective stays smooth.
2. **Step.** One trust run over every parameter, structural and Cholesky,
   on the frozen nodes, with the exact Hessian where the model has second
   derivatives. The nodes of the mu-referenced fixed effects (random
   intercepts whose formula covers every condition with data, covariates
   constant within a group) are frozen in $\phi = X\beta + \eta$: their
   data term does not depend on $\beta$ between rebuilds, so they need no
   sensitivities, and the frozen nodes stay accurate over larger steps.
3. The stage ends when a Newton step on the rebuilt nodes would lower
   $-2\log L$ by less than `tolDecrement`.

`method = "quadrature"` runs FOCEI to convergence first and starts from
its $\psi$ and $\hat\eta_i$: FOCEI is the fast Laplace E-step that
bootstraps, the quadrature the accurate one that refines.

At the estimate an importance-sampling certificate checks every group:
a multivariate $t_5$ proposal at the mode and conditional covariance,
evaluated on randomly shifted lattice points, gives $-2\log L_i$ with a
standard error and the Pareto shape of its weights. A group is flagged
when the two values differ by more than three standard errors plus the
error its level allows, or when the Pareto shape exceeds 0.7
(`fit$certificate`).

## Closed-form omega update

The full-data log-density of the random effects is

$$
\log p(\eta \mid \Omega) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_i \left[ \log |\Omega| \;+\; \eta_i^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_i \right] \;+\; \text{const}.
$$

Taking the expectation under the current grid replaces
$\eta_i \eta_i^\top$ by its posterior expectation $\hat M_i$. Setting
the derivative with respect to $\Omega$ to zero gives the sufficient
statistic

$$
S \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \hat M_i.
$$

The effect formulas make $\Omega$ block diagonal: the random effects
of one ID, or of one term without an ID, form a full block, the others
are independent. Per block the maximiser is the block of $S$ itself,
and `R/nlmePrior.R::.updateNormal` reads its Cholesky factor off into
the parameters `omega_<a>_<b>` (log on the diagonal); with some entries
fixed it maximises over the others. laplaceEM and SAEM take this
M-step; the quadrature fit moves the Cholesky parameters in its trust
step instead.

## Diagnostics

A quadrature fit holds `stageTrace`, one row per rebuild with the stage
level, the objective value, the Newton decrement, the highest level and
the number of nodes, `etaCov`, the posterior covariance
$\hat M_i - \hat m_i \hat m_i^\top$ of every group, and `certificate`. `plotTrace(fit)` shows the trace.
`plotRandomEffects(fit)` overlays the histograms of the modes with the
fitted $\mathcal{N}(0, \Omega_{kk})$.

# Stochastic Approximation EM (SAEM)

## Why a stochastic E-step

FOCEI and the sparse grid are both *deterministic* approximations of
the same E-step expectation, and both inherit a structural weakness
from that choice. FOCEI assumes $q_i$ is Gaussian and is biased
whenever it is not. The sparse grid drops that assumption, but only by
placing nodes: the rule stays anchored on the local Gaussian, so a
posterior whose mass sits away from $\hat\eta_i$ is resolved only by
raising the level, and the node count $B$ grows with the level at a
rate that steepens with $K$. Every node costs one ODE solve. Past
$K \approx 4$ that is the binding constraint.

Monte Carlo has the complementary profile. Drawing
$\eta_i \sim q_i$ needs no Gaussian assumption, is not anchored at the
mode, and costs the same per draw whether $K$ is 2 or 20. The price is
that the E-step is now an estimate with variance, and the clean
Jensen argument of Section 4 no longer applies per iteration.

The naive fix is MCEM: replace
$Q_i(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$ by an average over $M$ draws. It works,
but badly. The Monte-Carlo error must vanish for the iteration to
converge, so $M$ has to grow without bound, and every draw is
discarded at the end of the iteration that produced it. SAEM (Delyon,
Lavielle and Moulines, 1999) is the observation that this is
wasteful: the averaging does not have to happen *within* an iteration,
it can happen *across* iterations. Take very few draws per iteration,
even a single one, and let a Robbins-Monro recursion accumulate them.
The Monte-Carlo error is then averaged out along the trajectory rather
than at each point of it.

## Sufficient statistics: why the recursion is legitimate

SAEM is not "EM with noise added". It rests on an exponential-family
structure that the NLME random-effects block happens to have exactly.

Suppose the complete-data likelihood is in the curved exponential
family,

$$
\log p(y, \eta \mid \psi) \;=\; -\phi(\psi) \;+\; \langle S(y, \eta),\, \nu(\psi) \rangle,
$$

for a sufficient statistic $S$. Then the E-step never needs the whole
function $\eta \mapsto \log p(y, \eta \mid \psi)$; it needs one
vector, $\mathbb{E}_{q}[S(y, \eta)]$, and the M-step is a fixed map
$s \mapsto \hat\psi(s)$ applied to it. An expectation of a *fixed*
statistic is precisely the kind of object Robbins-Monro stochastic
approximation was built to estimate. That is the whole idea: replace
$\mathbb{E}_q[S]$ by the recursion

$$
s_k \;=\; s_{k-1} \;+\; \gamma_k \left( S(y, \eta^{(k)}) - s_{k-1} \right),
\qquad \eta^{(k)} \sim q(\cdot \mid \psi^{(k-1)}),
$$

and set $\psi^{(k)} = \hat\psi(s_k)$. Under the Robbins-Monro
conditions below, $s_k$ converges almost surely and the iterates
converge to a stationary point of the marginal likelihood $\ell$.

In our model the random-effects block fits this template exactly.
With $\eta_i \mid \Omega \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Omega)$,

$$
\log p(\eta \mid \Omega) \;=\; -\tfrac{N}{2}\log|\Omega|
\;-\; \tfrac{1}{2} \left\langle \sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top,\; \Omega^{-1} \right\rangle
\;+\; \text{const},
$$

which is exponential-family in $\Omega$ with sufficient statistic
$\sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top$, and the M-step map $\hat\psi(s)$ is the
*same closed form* the deterministic path already uses:
$S = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top$ fed to
`.updateNormal`. So the $\Omega$ update under SAEM is textbook SAEM,
and it is the same CM-2 as in the quadrature path with one
substitution: the posterior second moment $\hat M_i$, which the grid
computes by softmax-weighted quadrature, is replaced by the raw outer
product $\eta_i \eta_i^\top$ of a *draw*.

The structural block $\theta$ fits the template where it is
mu-referenced: a fixed effect $\beta$ that enters a symbol only through
$\phi_i = D_i \beta + \eta_i$, with $D_i$ constant within the group
(`.muReference`). Holding $\phi_i$ while $\beta$ moves, the data term does
not depend on $\beta$, and $\beta$ and $\Omega$ follow in closed form from
averaged sufficient statistics of $\phi$: the generalised least-squares
$\beta$ (`.glsFixedEffects`) alternated with `.updateNormal`. The other
structural parameters (error model, parameters without a random effect)
enter through the ODE solution and admit no sufficient statistic of fixed
dimension. During burn-in they take one `trust()` step per iteration on the
complete-data objective at the drawn etas. During averaging its gradient
$g_k$ and Hessian $H_k$ at $\theta_k$ enter a Robbins-Monro average of its
quadratic models,

$$
A_k = A_{k-1} + \gamma_k (H_k - A_{k-1}), \qquad
c_k = c_{k-1} + \gamma_k (H_k \theta_k - g_k - c_{k-1}),
$$

and $\theta$ takes the Newton step on $\tfrac12 \theta^\top A_k \theta - c_k^\top \theta$,
at most one unit long. At the fixed point the averaged gradient vanishes,
the score of the marginal by Fisher's identity. Averaging the Newton steps
of the single draws would instead solve $\mathbb{E}[H^{-1} g] = 0$, which
misses the score wherever the curvature differs between draws, for a
residual scale towards the harmonic mean of the residual sums of squares.

## The three steps

Each SAEM iteration $k$ performs:

* **S-step (simulation).** For each group draw
  $\eta_i^{(k)} \sim q_i(\eta \mid y_i, \psi^{(k-1)})$, the target $\Phi_i$
  of the FOCEI section. The value of $\Phi_i$ for all groups comes from one
  prediction without sensitivities (`.groupDensity`). A few random-walk
  Metropolis steps from the previous draw are followed by independence
  proposals from $N(\hat\eta_i, 1.5\,(H_i/2)^{-1})$ at the conditional modes,
  refreshed every few iterations. Every proposal keeps $q_i$ invariant, so
  the short chain suffices (Markov-chain SAEM, Kuhn and Lavielle, 2004).
  The random numbers come from the session stream.
* **A-step (approximation).** Update the sufficient statistics of
  $\phi$ and $\eta$, $S \leftarrow S + \gamma_k(s(\eta^{(k)}) - S)$.
* **M-step.** $\beta$ and $\Omega$ in closed form from $S$, the other
  structural parameters by the step above.

## The two phases

The step size $\gamma_k$ separates the two jobs of the algorithm. During
burn-in $\gamma_k = 1$: no memory, the iterates move at full step toward
the region of interest. Draws of chains that have not mixed yet
underestimate the spread of the random effects, so a variance of
$\Omega$ shrinks by at most 5 % per iteration (simulated annealing, as in
Lavielle 2014). Burn-in ends when no parameter drifts: the slope of every
parameter over the last `window` iterations is below twice its standard
error.

During averaging $\gamma_k = k^{-0.7}$ satisfies the Robbins-Monro
conditions $\sum_k \gamma_k = \infty$ and $\sum_k \gamma_k^2 < \infty$, and the
estimate is the mean of the iterates after the first `window`
(Polyak-Ruppert averaging). Averaging ends when the expected increase of
$-2\log L$ from the Monte Carlo error is below `mcTol`,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Delta(-2\log L)\big] \;\approx\;
\operatorname{tr}\!\big(I_c\, V\, I_c\, I_{\text{obs}}^{-1}\big),
$$

with $V$ the batch-means covariance of the single-draw M-steps, $I_c$ the
complete-data information and $I_{\text{obs}}$ half the Hessian of the
marginal by quadrature at the end of burn-in. `converged` reports both
rules; `nBurnin` and `nEM` are maxima.

## What it costs

SAEM removes the Laplace bias and the node explosion, and pays for it
in three places worth stating plainly:

* **No monotone improvement.** The Section 4 guarantee needs the exact
  E-step. SAEM's convergence is asymptotic and almost-sure, not
  per-iteration; a trace that goes briefly the wrong way is not a bug.
* **No OFV from the algorithm.** SAEM never forms the marginal
  likelihood; it only ever touches the complete-data objective. dMod2
  therefore evaluates the marginal *once* at the converged point using
  the quadrature machinery at level $K{+}2$, so `fit$value` remains
  directly comparable to the FOCEI and quadrature OFVs.
* **Standard errors come from that final evaluation**, i.e. from the
  quadrature observed information, not from a stochastic-information
  (Louis / Fisher-identity) accumulation along the SAEM path.

The regime where SAEM wins is the one that breaks the other two: high
$K$, strongly nonlinear models, and posteriors that are skewed,
heavy-tailed, or multimodal.

# Laplace random effects

A random term `(1 | gr(cellline, dist = laplace()))` gives the deviations
$\eta$ the density $\tfrac{\lambda}{2} e^{-\lambda |\eta|}$ per group and
coordinate. Its mode is exactly zero unless the data pull it away, so the
fit sorts shared from group-specific parameters, with one strength
$\lambda$ per term estimated from all its deviations. Clusters of groups
with equal values are the Dirichlet-process random effects below.

## The approximate marginal

`R/nlmeLaplace.R::.laplaceModes` finds the joint mode $\hat\eta$ of all
deviations by `trustL1()`: the data $-2\log L$, the normal prior, $2\lambda|\eta|$
per Laplace coordinate and $\eta^2/\tau^2$ per spike-and-slab coordinate.
Around the mode the data term $D_i$ of group $i$ is expanded to second
order with gradient $g$ and Gauss-Newton curvature $H$ (`.gnCurvature`).

**Normal etas.** At the mode the gradient of the data term and the normal
prior vanishes in the normal etas $N$, so they integrate out exactly on
the quadratic model. With $H_{NN}$ including the prior precision
$2\Omega^{-1}$, they leave the volume $\log|H_{NN}/2|$ and, for the sparse
coordinates $S$ (Laplace and spike and slab), the Schur complement

$$
S_i \;=\; H_{SS} - H_{SN} H_{NN}^{-1} H_{NS},
$$

a Gaussian factor of precision $P_i = S_i/2$ and centre
$m_i = \hat\eta_S - S_i^{-1} g_S$ per group. The value is

$$
-2 \log L \;\approx\; \sum_i \Big[ D_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log|H_{NN}/2| - \tfrac12 g_S^\top S_i^{-1} g_S \Big]
+ \text{prior}(\hat\eta_N) \;-\; 2 \log I,
$$

with $I = \int \prod_i e^{-\frac12 (\eta_i - m_i)^\top P_i (\eta_i - m_i)}\, p(\eta)\, d\eta$
over the sparse coordinates of all groups and $p$ their prior.

**Sparse coordinates by mean field.** $I$ factorises only when the $P_i$
are diagonal. `.sparseMeanField` replaces the posterior of the sparse
coordinates by a product of factors: a Laplace stem over all groups, a
Dirichlet-process stem over all groups, and the spike-and-slab stems of a group
jointly. A factor $b$ sees the others
through their posterior means $\mu$ only: its quadratic is
$\tfrac12 (\eta_b - \tilde m_b)^\top P_{bb} (\eta_b - \tilde m_b)$ with the shifted
centre

$$
\tilde m_b \;=\; m_b - P_{bb}^{-1} r_b, \qquad r_b = \sum_{c \ne b} P_{bc} (\mu_c - m_c),
$$

and it is integrated exactly there (`.factorIntegral`: the normal-Laplace
integral `.normalLaplace` in closed form by the scaled complementary error
function, the subset sum `.slabSubsets`, the partition sum
`.slabPartition`). The factors are updated in turn until the means stop
changing. With $d = \mu - m$ the result

$$
\log I \;\ge\; \sum_b \log Z_b(\tilde m_b) \;+\; \sum_{b<c} d_b^\top P_{bc}\, d_c
\;+\; \tfrac12 \sum_b r_b^\top P_{bb}^{-1} r_b
$$

is the variational lower bound of $\log I$ over factorised posteriors, the
Gibbs-Bogoliubov bound. It is exact when the factors are uncoupled and
loses the correlated fluctuations between factors otherwise; in the
purely Gaussian case these are the correlation part of the determinant.

**Coupled factors by expectation consistent.** Where the data couple
factors, the default is the expectation-consistent approximation (Opper
and Winther 2005; `.sparseExpectation`). It writes the integrand as the
product of the factor priors $f$ and the Gaussian coupling $g$, and looks
at it in two tractable ways: $q \propto f\, c$, the factors exact under a
diagonal Gaussian cavity $c$, one normal per coordinate, and
$r \propto g\, t$, the coupling exact under diagonal Gaussian sites $t$.
The sites are set so that $q$ and $r$ have the same mean and variance in
every coordinate, and

$$
\log I \;\approx\; \log \int f\, c \;+\; \log \int g\, t \;-\; \log \int c\, t .
$$

The first integral is `.factorIntegral` at the cavity, the other two are
Gaussian. In the language of statistical physics the cavity is the
effective field of the rest of the system on one factor, solved
self-consistently with its fluctuations; the result is exact without
coupling and for Gaussian factors. The fixed point is found by updating the
factors in turn with adaptive damping, halving a step that would make a
cavity precision non-positive, and starting each evaluation from the sites
of the last. For two coupled stems of four or five groups its error is 3 to
15 times smaller than that of mean field, the more so the stronger the
coupling; it is not a bound. The sites are iterated to a relative change
of $10^{-8}$. The iteration can fail, mostly where the posterior is strongly
multimodal, sharply separated clusters with precise data. Where it fails at
a point of a fit, that trust run is abandoned and starts again by mean
field, and from its optimum a run by expectation consistent follows, in
which a trial point where it fails counts as infeasible; `fit$coupling` reports which integral the result is,
and `control$laplace$coupling = "meanField"` keeps the bound throughout.

## Exact gradient

The bound is stationary in the factors, so its derivatives in $m$, $P$
and the hyperparameters hold them fixed:

$$
\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial m_i} = P_i d_i, \qquad
\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial P_i} = -\tfrac12 \big(d_i d_i^\top + \operatorname{Cov}_q(\eta_i)\big),
$$

with the factor covariances block diagonal, and the derivative in a
hyperparameter is the expectation of the derivative of its log prior
under the factors (Fisher's identity per factor). The
expectation-consistent value is stationary in the sites, so the same
holds with $d_i = \mu^r_i - m_i$ and the covariance of $r$, which is full
within a group, and with the hyperparameter derivatives of the factors at
the cavity. These pass through
$m = \hat\eta - S^{-1} g$ and $P = S/2$ to $g$, to $S$ and through the Schur
complement to $H$ and $\Omega$, then with $\partial g/\partial\psi$ from the
exact Hessian of the data term, $\partial H/\partial\psi$ and
$\partial H/\partial\eta$ from second derivatives of the prediction and the
error model, and the shift of the mode from the stationarity of its free
coordinates (normal and slab etas, Laplace coordinates away from zero),
$C^\top (\nabla_\eta D + \text{subgradient}) = 0$,

$$
\frac{d z}{d \psi} \;=\; -\left(C^\top \nabla^2_\eta D\, C\right)^{-1} C^\top \nabla^2_{\eta\psi} D .
$$

The gradient is exact for the approximate marginal; coordinates at zero
do not move. The same shift with the derivative of the subgradient gives
the derivative in $\lambda$, and it gives the first-order start of the
inner modes at the next trial point.

## Strengths and the trust region

The closed-form M-step of a hyperparameter $h$ minimises the expected
complete-data objective $Q(h) = \mathbb{E}[-2\log p(\eta \mid h)]$ at the
current posterior moments, for a strength
$\lambda = n / \sum \mathbb{E}|\eta|$ over the $n$ deviations of a term. Near
the optimum such a step is a gradient step scaled by the complete-data
information $I_c$, the information the deviations would give if they were
observed, while the data hold only $I_{\text{obs}} = I_c - I_{\text{mis}}$;
the error shrinks by the fraction of missing information per iteration
(Dempster, Laird and Rubin 1977),

$$
e_{k+1} \approx I_c^{-1} I_{\text{mis}}\, e_k .
$$

A strength estimated from a few groups gets almost all of its information
through their uncertain deviations, the rate is close to one, and EM alone
is slow. A Newton step on the curvature of $Q$ at the current point is no
better far from the optimum: on the unbounded scale $u = \log\lambda$ the
M-step lies at $u^* = \log(n / \sum \mathbb{E}|\eta|)$, while the Newton step
is $e^{u^* - u} - 1$, a step of $-1$ where $u^*$ lies five below and one of
$147$ where it lies five above.

`R/nlmeLaplace.R::.fitLaplace` moves all parameters in one trust region,
the hyperparameters on their unbounded scale $u$ ($\log\lambda$,
$\log\tau$, $\log c$, $\operatorname{logit} p$), with the exact gradient of
the marginal. For the fixed parameters the model Hessian is the
Gauss-Newton Schur complement over all random effects, the sparse ones at
the curvature of their posterior: a factor with posterior covariance $C$
and data curvature $S_{ff}$ of $-2\log L$ gets the prior curvature
$2C^{-1} - S_{ff}$, under expectation consistent the sites,
$2\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda)$. With normal random effects alone this is the
Schur complement of FOCEI. The Schur complement over the free modes alone
would not do: a fixed parameter whose deviations are free under a Laplace
prior has no curvature there, since the data see only their sum and the
prior has none, and its curvature jumps to that of the data where the
deviations sit at zero. For every hyperparameter the model Hessian is the
secant of the complete-data gradient to its M-step,

$$
B_h = \frac{\partial_u Q(u)}{u - u^*}, \qquad
\partial_u Q = 2\Bigl(\lambda \sum \mathbb{E}|\eta| - n\Bigr), \quad
2\Bigl(F - \frac{\mathbb{E}\sum v^2}{\tau^2}\Bigr), \quad
-2\,(F - G p), \quad
-2\Bigl(F - \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{c}{c+i}\Bigr),
$$

with $F$ the expected number of slab deviations or of clusters off the
population value and $G$ the groups. $Q$ is convex in $u$ for all four, so
$B_h > 0$, and a Newton step on $B_h$ is the exact M-step. Where $u = u^*$,
$B_h$ is the curvature of $Q$, the complete-data information

$$
2\lambda \sum \mathbb{E}|\eta|, \qquad
4\, \frac{\mathbb{E}\sum v^2}{\tau^2}, \qquad
2 G\, p (1 - p), \qquad
2 \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{c\, i}{(c+i)^2}.
$$

A BFGS correction from the accepted steps learns the missing information
and the curvature between fixed parameters and hyperparameters (Lange
1995, Jamshidian and Jennrich 1997). Far from the optimum it is small, and
a step is an EM step in the hyperparameters and a Gauss-Newton step in the
fixed parameters, at one evaluation of the marginal instead of an inner
fit; near the optimum the model approaches the Hessian of the marginal and
the steps converge superlinearly. The model has the gradient of the
marginal and a bounded Hessian, which is all the convergence of a trust
region needs (Conn, Gould and Toint 2000), and its ratio of actual to
predicted reduction alone sets the step: there is no number of EM
iterations to choose. The trust region stops as the outer one of FOCEI,
at a predicted reduction below `mtol`; a run that stops short starts again
with a fresh correction while the runs lower $-2\log L$. A multistart
guards against local optima. Neither model Hessian is the Hessian of the
marginal, which would need the curvature of the integral over the sparse
coordinates: such a fit reports none, its standard errors come from the
scores of the groups (section Standard errors of sparse fits).

# Spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process random effects

A term `(1 | gr(cellline, dist = spikeSlab()))` lets every deviation be
exactly zero (the spike) or a draw from $N(0, \tau^2)$ (the slab); every
group deviates with probability $p$, independently. With
`gr(cellline, dist = dirichletProcess())` the groups of a symbol and the population
value form clusters; the cluster of the population value has deviation
zero and every other cluster one common deviation from the slab. The fit
estimates $p$ or the concentration $c$ and $\tau$ by marginal maximum
likelihood, one fit without a penalty to scan.

## The prior of the clusters

The partitions of the $G$ groups and the population value (the anchor)
have the Ewens distribution of the Chinese restaurant process with
concentration $c$ and the anchor seated first: a group joins an
existing cluster with probability proportional to its size, the anchor
counted, or opens a new one with probability proportional to $c$,

$$
\Pr(\pi) \;=\; \frac{c^{K-1} \prod_{b \in \pi} (n_b - 1)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{G} (c + i)},
$$

$K$ the number of clusters and $n_b$ their sizes. The prior depends on
the sizes only: it is exchangeable in the groups, independent of their
order and of the data, and consistent in $G$, so that leaving out a group
gives the prior of the others. $c \to 0$ puts every group at the
population value, $c \to \infty$ every group in a cluster of its own;
the expected number of free clusters is $\sum_{i=1}^{G} c / (c + i)$.

## The approximate marginal

The data term is expanded as for Laplace random effects, around the mode
under the slab alone, $\eta^\top \eta / \tau^2$ in the inner objective. That
mode is smooth in the parameters, so the marginal does not jump where
the most probable structure changes. Under the expansion every structure
is a Gaussian integral.

**Spike and slab.** The spike-and-slab coordinates of a group are integrated together on
their precision $P$ and centre $m$ (`R/nlmeSpikeSlab.R::.slabSubsets`):
over the subsets $F$ of slab coordinates, with $b = P m$ and
$Q = P_{FF} + \operatorname{diag}(1/\tau^2)$,

$$
I \;=\; \sum_F p^{|F|} (1 - p)^{K - |F|}\,
\frac{\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12 m^\top P m + \tfrac12 b_F^\top Q^{-1} b_F\big)}
{|Q|^{1/2}\, \tau^{|F|}},
$$

$2^K$ terms for the $K$ coordinates of a group.

**Clusters.** Per symbol, on the factors $(a_g, m_g)$ of its $G$ groups, a
cluster $T$ of groups contributes $-C/2$ to the log integrand if it holds
the anchor and

$$
-\tfrac12 \log(1 + \tau^2 A) - \tfrac{C}{2} + \frac{B^2}{2 (A + 1/\tau^2)},
\qquad A = \sum_T a_g,\ B = \sum_T a_g m_g,\ C = \sum_T a_g m_g^2,
$$

otherwise. The sum over all set partitions is a recursion over the
subsets of the $G + 1$ elements (`src/dirichletProcess_kernel.cpp`): with $F(S)$
the sum over the partitions of $S$ of the products of their cluster
weights,

$$
F(S) \;=\; \sum_{T \subseteq S,\ \min S \in T} w(T)\, F(S \setminus T),
$$

$3^{G+1}$ terms, exact for up to 14 groups. The posterior probability that
$T$ is a cluster is $w(T) F(U \setminus T) / F(U)$, $U$ the full set; the
posterior moments, the M-step statistics and the derivatives follow from
these probabilities.

## Gradient and M-step

Fisher's identity gives the derivatives of $\log I$ in $m$, in $P$ (or
$a$) and in $p$, $c$ and $\tau$ from the posterior moments, and the chain
through $g$, $H$ and the mode is that of the Laplace case. The mode
shifts with $\tau$ through the slab term, not with $p$ or $c$. The M-steps
are

$$
\tau^2 = \frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{\text{free clusters}} v^2\big]}{\mathbb{E}[\text{free clusters}]},
\qquad
p = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\text{deviating groups}]}{G},
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{c}{c + i} = \mathbb{E}[\text{free clusters}],
$$

summed over the symbols of a term; the last equation is increasing in
$c$ and solved by Newton's method (`.ewensConcentration`). They set the
curvature of $p$, $c$ and $\tau$ in the trust region with the fixed
parameters, as for the strengths (section Strengths and the trust region).

## Many groups: SAEM

The exact partition sum is limited to 14 groups. `method = "saem"` draws
the partition instead (`R/nlmeSaem.R::.fitSaemDirichlet`). Per iteration a
Gibbs sweep moves every group to an existing cluster, with probability
proportional to its size times the data likelihood of the group at the
cluster value, or to one of two auxiliary clusters with values from the
slab, with probability proportional to $c/2$ times the likelihood there
(Neal 2000, algorithm 8); the likelihoods of all groups at a value come
from one prediction. Random-walk Metropolis steps then move the cluster
values. Every group starts in a cluster of its own at its mode under the
slab alone, so the sampler merges clusters rather than finding deviations
by draws from the slab, and during burn-in $c$ and $\tau$ shrink by at
most 5 % per iteration. The averaged number of free clusters and sum of
their squared values give $\tau$ and $c$ by the M-steps above. The
reported structure is the most frequent partition of the late draws.

Its $-2\log L$ comes from sequential importance sampling under the
expansion (`.dirichletImportance`): the groups are seated one after the
other, each joins clusters with probability proportional to the prior
times its predictive given the groups seated before, the cluster values
of a particle having a joint normal posterior; the product of the
predictive normalisers is unbiased for $I$, and its spread over the
particles gives the standard error `valueSE`. Coupled stems of a group are
seated together, so no factorisation enters.

## The reported structure

The fit reports the most probable structure, the recursion with the
maximum for the sum: deviations of the spike are exactly zero, every
free cluster has its posterior mean, and `fit$random` holds the cluster
of every group (0 for the population value) and its posterior
probability of zero.

## Standard errors of sparse fits

With Laplace and spike-and-slab random effects the marginal is a sum over
independent groups and the conditions without random effects,
$-2\log L = \sum_g \ell_g + \ell_0$. The mode, the curvature and the
integral of a group depend on its data alone, and the shift of the mode
with the parameters is block diagonal by groups, so the exact gradient of
the marginal splits into the exact gradients $\nabla \ell_g$ of the
groups. With the scores $s_g = -\tfrac12 \nabla \ell_g$ and their mean
$\bar s$, the empirical information is

$$
I = \frac{G}{G-1} \sum_{g=1}^{G} (s_g - \bar s)(s_g - \bar s)^\top + \tfrac12 H_0,
$$

$H_0$ the Hessian of $\ell_0$; `fit$information` holds it and `vcov()`
inverts it. At the optimum the scores sum to $-\tfrac12 \nabla \ell_0$,
and the centring removes that direction exactly: the rank of the first
term is at most $G - 1$, so the information needs more groups than
parameters, and where it does not span every direction `vcov()` is an
error and the standard errors are `NA`. Under `dirichletProcess()` the
partition couples the groups, the marginal is no sum over groups, and a
fit has neither a Hessian nor an empirical information;
`confint(method = "profile")` gives intervals.

# End-user API

The walkthrough on the Theophylline data is `demo("TheophNLME")`,
rendered to `examples/TheophNLME.md`, with the comparison against
`nlmixr2` FOCEI.

## Random effects on the parameter transformation

```{r trafo}
library(dMod2)
trafo <- branch(define(NULL, "x <- x", x = getParameters(model)), table = covariates)
trafo <- insert(trafo, "x <- exp(x)", x = c("ka", "cl", "v"))   # log parameters
trafo <- insert(trafo,
  ka ~ 1 + (1 | p | ID),                     # normal, correlated with cl
  cl ~ wt + (1 + dose | p | ID),             # covariate and random slope
  v  ~ 1 + (1 | ID))                         # independent
p <- P(trafo, compile = TRUE)
randomEffects(p)
```

The branch table has one row per condition; the column `ID` gives the
group of a condition, so a subject may own several conditions.
`gr(ID, dist = laplace())`, `gr(ID, dist = spikeSlab())` or
`gr(ID, dist = dirichletProcess())` in place of `ID` makes a term Laplace,
spike and slab or clusters.

## Fit

```{r fit}
obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = err)          # or normT(..., df = 4)
fit <- em(obj, randomEffects(p), init = c(ka = 0, cl = 0, v = 3, sigma = log(0.5)))
fit <- em(obj, randomEffects(p), init = fit$argument, method = "quadrature")
fit <- msem(obj, randomEffects(p), init = c(ka = 0, cl = 0, v = 3, sigma = log(0.5)),
            fits = 20, cores = 4)
```

`init` needs the parameters that are neither random effects nor
created by the effect formulas, which start at 0; the standard
deviations start at `control$sd`. `method` is `"focei"` (default),
`"quadrature"`, `"laplaceEM"` or `"saem"`; Laplace and spike-and-slab
terms are fitted by `"focei"`, Dirichlet-process terms by `"focei"` or
`"saem"`.

## Inspecting the fit

```{r diagnostics}
summary(fit)                         # estimates with SE and RSE, Omega, shrinkage; seMethod
fit$omega                            # standard deviations and correlations with SE
fit$random                           # modes per group with conditional SE
fit$strengths                        # Laplace strengths
fit$slab                             # prob or concentration and tau
logLik(fit); AIC(fit); BIC(fit)
residuals(fit, type = "CWRES")
predict(fit, type = "population")
confint(fit, parm = "cl", method = "profile")
anova(fit0, fit)
simulate(fit, nsim = 10)
plot(fit); plotCombined(fit); plotResiduals(fit); plotRandomEffects(fit)
plotTrace(fitQuadrature)
```

`value` is the $-2\log L$ with every constant of the data;
`valueNonmem` $= \text{value} - N_{\text{obs}}\log(2\pi)$ is comparable
with the NONMEM `OBJ`.
